rss.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
rss.summary: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not (yet?) available as open weights. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up. Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one: I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4. It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look. I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark. rss.title: Ladybird's first alpha release
rss.summary: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS . This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool): Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script , thanks Claude): Ladybird (72925) [240 MB] └── Hub (72926) [61 MB] ├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB] ├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB] ├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB] ├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB] ├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB] ├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB] ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB] ├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB] ├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB] ├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB] ├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB] ├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB] ├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB] └── WebContent (73185) [60 MB] Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site). I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool . It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too. The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite , which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error: undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages') I filed an issue about this , then found a FIXME annotation in the source code. The October explosion The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI , describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex. Here's the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months: That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements. This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark , they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari! How did they do that? Coding agents: Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing . I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October. Should you use Ladybird? Here's what Andreas says about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser: This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details. We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird! Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts. I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings. rss.title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
rss.summary: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo, an open-source runtime for Linux. It helps teams protect running systems while they roll out patches.
rss.text_excerpt:
OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart. We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day. Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline. Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running. Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems. OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities: Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it. Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed. Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. rss.title: Richpanel helps companies automate 50% of support in 30 days
rss.summary: Richpanel uses GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol to equip its AI support agents with tools and procedures, and GPT-6 Luna for their conversations.
rss.text_excerpt:
Beyond knowing how to answer a customer’s request, AI support agents need to be able to execute a solution. And for that, they need access to the right tools and instructions. According to Richpanel CEO Amit RG, human support agents can use 20 or 30 tools to serve a customer, and the procedures they follow may never have been written down. Richpanel ⁠ (opens in a new window) solves that using OpenAI models to both set up the tools and procedures AI support agents need to act and handle customer conversations. “The intelligence is no longer the bottleneck. It’s everything around it.” —Amit RG, CEO, Richpanel Deploying a support agent often requires a forward-deployed engineer to connect the agent to a customer’s systems and define how it should work. Amit saw that many companies didn’t have engineers to spare and asked himself, “What if that forward-deployed engineer itself was an AI agent?” So Richpanel built it: an AI manager to handle agent setup. Customers began calling it Boss AI. It writes procedures and defines how Richpanel’s frontline support agent, copilot, and quality-assurance agent call the tools they need. Richpanel uses GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol for Boss AI, prioritizing accuracy when building the tools and procedures its other agents will follow. Richpanel designs the frontline agent to handle hundreds of thousands of conversations, making the cost of each interaction an important part of model selection. It uses GPT‑6 Luna and other OpenAI models for that work. Amit says Richpanel takes the same approach to its copilot and quality-assurance agents. “What matters is a balance of cost and intelligence,” Amit says. Richpanel’s customers may already use low-cost outsourced support. Automating their operations has to make financial sense against that starting point. Amit credits OpenAI with making models available that can handle long context and longer tasks while remaining cost efficient. Richpanel can use deeper reasoning to prepare its support agents and more economical models to run the conversations that follow. “OpenAI models can run these long-context, longer-horizon tasks while still being very cost efficient.” —Amit RG, CEO, Richpanel At the time of the October 2026 interview, Amit said Richpanel had completed approximately 300 AI customer-support deployments over the previous six months. rss.title: datasette-charts 0.1a0
rss.summary: Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set. I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible. rss.title: Perplexity and Intelligence
rss.summary: How perplexity measures progress in AI models, and why it could help developers establish a shared approach to evaluating emerging capabilities.
rss.text_excerpt:
From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently ⁠ (opens in a new window) , predictor) on a very large corpus of data. 1 I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared ⁠ (opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts. A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “ an alien mind ⁠ ”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation. The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset. 2 , 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. rss.title: Lessons from 12 Evals: Where They Break and What to Measure Instead
rss.summary: How benchmarks are built, the bugs they have, and hot takes on what should change.
rss.text_excerpt:
As models ship faster, eval scores are often the first thing we learn about a new model. But how much weight should we put in them? In eight of twelve public evals studied, there’s evidence the grader failed work that should have passed. And even when the grader gets it right, many benchmarks measure what’s easy rather than what matters, and should instead focus on reliability, work velocity, multi-turn collaboration, etc. Here, we’ll cover the common patterns and principles, the errors models make, and where current benchmarks fall short. I’ll also share what we’re getting wrong and what should change, including why average pass rate isn’t enough and why dollars are the wrong measure of cost. Finally, we’ll walk through twelve evals: four on coding and science, six on knowledge work, and two on browsing and computer use. By the end, you’ll know what to trust in a benchmark and what to question. Patterns: How eval tasks are built and maintained # Most eval tasks share four components: Instruction: A prompt that sounds like a real user’s request. The agent gets it once at the start and typically can’t ask clarifying questions. Environment: The workspace where the agent operates. Typically comes with the files, software, and services needed. For coding, this is usually a container with a repo at a specific git commit. For knowledge work, it might be a VM with installed software, simulated business apps, or a folder of documents. Grader: This decides whether the work passes. It can be deterministic code (tests and assertions over the final output or environment state), an LLM judge scoring a rubric of yes/no criteria, or a mix of both. Everything runs on your own GPU: [Qwen-Image-2.1](https://huggingface.co/Qwen) on [stable-diffusion.cpp](https://github.com/leejet/stable-diffusion.cpp). No ComfyUI, no Python, no cloud rendering. ![EggLab panel](docs/panel.png) ## What it can do - **Chat with a design agent** that knows PhotoCraft: layers, masks, text, exports. - **Generate images** (quality 40-step or turbo 8-step LoRA) at up to 2048 px. - **Edit images** — reference photos, multi-reference compositions, transparent cut-outs. - **Place results** on the PhotoCraft canvas as layers, or export flat/layered files. - **Local-first** — models and renders stay on your disk; only chat text goes to the model provider you pick. ## Requirements - Windows 10 or 11 (x64) - **PhotoCraft** installed ([download free](https://getartcraft.com/)) — the canvas app EggLab drives; not bundled - ~25 GB free disk: engine (17 MB–1.5 GB depending on GPU) + models (~20 GB, your choice) - A GPU is strongly recommended: - NVIDIA → CUDA engine (fastest, ~1.4 GB download) - Any DX12 GPU → Vulkan engine (~29 MB) - CPU works but is slow - Internet for the engine download and the model downloads ## Install 1. Download **`EggLab-Setup-<version>.exe`** from [Releases](../../releases). 2. Windows SmartScreen will warn because the installer is not code-signed yet: **More info → Run anyway**. This is an unsigned-publisher warning, not a virus detection; verify `SHA256SUMS.txt` if you want to check the download. The fix and the signing options are in [docs/SIGNING.md](docs/SIGNING.md). 3. The installer copies the app (~77 MB) and downloads the engine that matches your GPU (SHA-256 verified, resumable; CUDA → Vulkan → CPU fallback if a download fails). 4. Launch EggLab and finish the setup wizard (below). `SHA256SUMS.txt` is attached to every release if you want to verify the download: ```powershell Get-ChildItem .\EggLab-Setup-*.exe | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 ``` ## First run ![EggLab setup](docs/setup.png) The wizard checks the four pieces EggLab needs: | Piece | What it is | What the wizard does | |---|---|---| | **PhotoCraft** | The canvas app ([download free](https://getartcraft.com/)) | Detects it, or lets you locate `photocraf

bloomery is a fast LLM inference server for mixture-of-experts models that are larger than the GPU.
It runs on NVIDIA cards, the DGX Spark included, and on Apple Silicon through Metal.
A drop-in llama-server, in Rust from the HTTP server down to the CUDA kernels.

0.3.16 release notes · Models · Serving · Agents · Evaluating · Contributing

```sh curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midagedev/bloomery/main/tools/release/install.sh | sh ~/.local/bin/bloomery-serve --hf unsloth/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-GGUF:Q4_K_M ``` These two commands install the latest release on Linux x86-64 with an NVIDIA GPU (or on Windows inside WSL2) and serve Qwen3-30B-A3B on port 8080; [Use](#use) sends it a first request. The same installer takes the GB10 archive on a DGX Spark ([DGX Spark](#dgx-spark-and-other-gb10-machines)), and an Apple Silicon Mac runs `bloomery-serve-metal` ([Apple Silicon](#apple-silicon)). Homebrew, Docker and the plain tarball are under [Install](#install). **From an agent.** Hand Claude Code, Codex or a script [`docs/agents.md`](docs/agents.md). The agent asks the machine what fits, then starts the model by its name. stdout carries JSON, and every refusal ends with a named exit code and the command to run next: ```sh bloomery-serve --recommend --json # what this machine serves, and the fastest variant of each bloomery-serve --model qwen3.8-flash-next --dry-run --json # the start it would run; downloads nothing bloomery-serve --model qwen3.8-flash-next --port 0 # start it: one JSON event a line, then "ready" with the url ``` On a Mac the server is `bloomery-serve-metal`, and the agent follows the "On a Mac" steps in the same page. # Hebo Gateway Roll your own AI gateway for full control over models, providers, routing logic, guardrails, observability and more ... ## 🐒 Overview Existing AI gateways like OpenRouter, Vercel AI Gateway, LiteLLM, and Portkey work out of the box, but they’re hard to extend once your needs go beyond configuration. Hebo Gateway is an open-source, embeddable AI gateway framework built to live inside your app. It gives you full control over providers, models, routing, and the request lifecycle. Learn more in our blog post: [Yet Another AI Gateway?](https://hebo.ai/blog/260127-hebo-gateway/) (`https://hebo.ai/blog/260127-hebo-gateway/`) ## 🍌 Features - 🌐 OpenAI-compatible `/chat/completions`, `/embeddings`, `/audio/transcriptions` & `/models` endpoints. - 💬 Open Responses `/responses` endpoint (stateless), including /conversations. - 🗨️ Anthropic-compatible `/messages` endpoint. - 🔌 Integrate into your existing Hono, Elysia, Next.js & TanStack apps. - 🧩 Provider registry compatible with any Vercel AI SDK providers. - 🧭 Canonical model IDs and parameter naming across providers. - 🗂️ Model catalog loaded from models.dev: new models need no gateway release. - 🪝 Hook system to customize routing, auth, rate limits, and shape responses. - 👁️ Observability via OTel GenAI semantic conventions (Langfuse-compatible). - 🧰 Low-level OpenAI-compatible schema, converters, and middleware helpers. ## 📦 Installation ```bash bun install @hebo-ai/gateway ``` ## ☰ Table of Contents - Quickstart - [Setup A Gateway Instance](#setup-a-gateway-instance) | [Mount Route Handlers](#mount-route-handlers) | [Call the Gateway](#call-the-gateway) - Configuration Reference - [Providers](#providers) | [Models](#models) | [Hooks](#hooks) | [Storage](#storage) | [Logger](#logger-settings) | [Observability](#observability) | [Advanced](#advanced-settings) - Framework Support - [ElysiaJS](#elysiajs) | [Hono](#hono) | [Next.js](#nextjs) | [TanStack Start](#tanstack-start) - Runtime Support - [Vercel Edge](#vercel-edge) | [Cloudflare Workers](#cloudflare-workers) | [Deno Deploy](#deno-deploy) | [AWS Lambda](#aws-lambda) - Endpoints - [/chat/completions](#chatcompletions) | [/embeddings](#embeddings) | [/audio/transcriptions](#audiotranscriptions) | [/models](#models) | [/responses](#responses) | [/messages](#messages) | [/conversations](#conversations) - OpenAI Extensions - [Reasoning](#reasoning) |

# Code Meeseeks **A desktop GUI for PR-Agent · A local, semi-automated AI code-review client for the individual reviewer** Graphical interface (GUI) for the community [PR-Agent](https://docs.pr-agent.ai/) · Electron desktop app · All data stays on your machine [![Electron](https://img.shields.io/badge/Electron-2B2E3A?logo=electron&logoColor=9FEAF9)](https://www.electronjs.org/) [![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-3178C6?logo=typescript&logoColor=white)](https://www.typescriptlang.org/) [![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3776AB?logo=python&logoColor=white)](https://www.python.org/) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/huhamhire/code-meeseeks?include_prereleases&sort=semver&label=release&color=4c9a40)](https://github.com/huhamhire/code-meeseeks/releases) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-181717?logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/) [![Bitbucket](https://img.shields.io/badge/Bitbucket-0052CC?logo=bitbucket&logoColor=white)](https://bitbucket.org/) [![GitLab](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitLab-FC6D26?logo=gitlab&logoColor=white)](https://gitlab.com/) Keywords：PR-Agent GUI · pr-agent desktop client · AI code review · Pull Request & Merge Request review · Bitbucket / GitHub reviewer tool · local / self-hosted / private deployment **English** · [简体中文](README.zh-CN.md) · [Website](https://huhamhire.github.io/code-meeseeks/)
--- Code Meeseeks (internal codename `meebox`) is a **desktop graphical interface (GUI)** for the command-line tool [pr-agent](https://docs.pr-agent.ai/): it packages AI-assisted code review into a desktop client — it fetches the PRs (Pull Requests / Merge Requests) awaiting your review, runs pr-agent locally to generate review comments, and lets the reviewer **confirm / edit each one** before publishing it back to the code hosting platform (GitHub / Bitbucket / GitLab). Core design stance: - **Human decides** — every comment must be confirmed / edited by the reviewer before it reaches the remote; the AI only drafts. - **Rules stay local** — the reviewer configures their own check rules, style preferences, and LLM provider. - **Data stays local** — repository mirrors, PR metadata, and comment drafts all live in a local working directory; friendly to corporate intranets.
